chapters.title: Chapter 6: Making It Work on a Real Portfolio

lessons.title: Constraints That Matter in Practice: No Short-Selling, Sector Caps, Turnover

children.text: Every chapter since Chapter 3 has flagged the same recurring warning: the unconstrained optimizer, left alone, will happily ask you to short a stock. This lesson stops treating that as a footnote and asks directly what an actual, implementable Indian portfolio looks like once the constraints real investors face are added back in.

body.text: A constraint can never make an optimization's result better. By definition, it only removes options the unconstrained version was allowed to use. The real question is never whether a constraint costs something in theoretical risk or return. It is how much, and whether that cost is worth paying for a portfolio you can actually run.

children.text: No Short-Selling: Why It's the Default in India

In India's cash equity market, a retail short sale must be squared off the same trading day. Carrying a genuine overnight short position in a stock is not available in the cash market at all, it requires shifting to futures and options instead, a different instrument with its own margin requirements, expiry dates, and risk profile entirely. Equity mutual funds face their own restriction: SEBI's regulations generally prohibit them from taking direct short positions in the underlying equity of a scheme. For most Indian retail and mutual-fund portfolios, the no-short-selling constraint is not an edge case worth footnoting. It is the realistic default.

body.caption: Chapter 3's optimization problem, with one more constraint added: every weight must be zero or positive.

children.text: Chapter 3, Lesson 5's five-stock frontier stayed feasible without shorting up to about 17.6% target return, the point where HUL's weight would otherwise cross below zero. Push the target return past that, and the true constrained solution simply holds HUL at exactly 0% and re-optimizes the remaining four stocks around it.

body.caption: Unconstrained versus constrained (long-only) solutions at the same target return

body.text: At 17.5%, the two solutions are essentially identical, since the unconstrained version barely wanted a short in the first place. At 18.0%, the gap becomes real: forcing HUL's weight to 0% instead of the -5.6% the unconstrained formula wanted costs an extra 0.13 percentage points of risk for the exact same 18% return. That gap is the concrete, priced-out cost of a rule the fund has to follow, not a rounding error.

Push the target return higher still, and a SECOND stock, Reliance in this five-stock universe, eventually wants to go negative too, even after HUL has already been floored at zero. Which assets hit their zero floor, and in what order, changes as the target return changes, and hand-adjusting the formula one dropped asset at a time stops being practical almost immediately. This is exactly why real portfolio tools solve constrained problems numerically, using a quadratic programming solver with bounds=(0, 1) added directly, as Chapter 3, Lesson 4's code already showed, rather than working the constrained algebra out by hand.

children.text: SEBI's mutual fund regulations generally cap most equity schemes at 10% of net asset value in any single company. Check that against Chapter 4, Lesson 2's tangency portfolio.

body.caption: The tangency portfolio against a 10% single-stock cap

body.text: Every single stock breaches a 10% cap. A real SEBI-regulated equity scheme could never actually hold Chapter 4's textbook tangency portfolio. It would need at least fifteen or twenty names just to stay compliant while keeping any resemblance to that risk-return profile, which is a large part of why real diversified equity funds hold far more than five stocks even when a concentrated five-stock book might, on paper, offer a better Sharpe ratio. Sector caps work identically: a fund mandate limiting any one sector to, say, 25% of the portfolio binds in exactly the same way, on top of the single-stock limit, whenever several names in the same sector could otherwise all earn large individual weights.

children.text: Turnover: the Cost of Chasing a Moving Target

Chapter 1, Lesson 3 already showed that weights drift on their own as prices move, with no trading required. Chasing the newly re-optimized "ideal" weights every time fresh data arrives means real, repeated trading, and every one of those trades costs something in India: brokerage, the Securities Transaction Tax (STT) on each transaction, the bid-ask spread, and capital gains tax, short-term or long-term depending on the holding period, triggered the moment a winning position is trimmed. A portfolio re-optimized every week in theory can lose more to these frictions than it gains from staying marginally closer to the frontier. Most real portfolios instead rebalance on a fixed schedule, or only once a position drifts past some tolerance band, deliberately trading a small amount of theoretical precision for meaningfully lower costs. Lesson 2 of this chapter covers exactly how that trade-off gets made.

body.title: Price the constraint
body.prompt: Using this lesson's table, how many percentage points of extra risk does the no-short-selling constraint cost at the 18.0% target return (unconstrained risk 18.84% versus constrained risk 18.97%)?
body.explanation: 18.97% - 18.84% = 0.13 percentage points. A small but real, precisely priced cost of following a rule the unconstrained formula was never asked to respect.

body.title: What a constraint can and cannot do
body.question: A fund's mandate prohibits short-selling. At a given target return, the unconstrained (theoretical) optimization wants to short one stock. What is true about the constrained (long-only) portfolio the fund can actually hold, for that SAME target return?
options: It will always have LOWER risk than the unconstrained solution, since avoiding shorts is inherently safer
It will have risk equal to or HIGHER than the unconstrained solution, never lower, since the constraint only removes options that were available before
It will always achieve a higher expected return for the same risk
The constraint has no effect on risk, only on which specific stocks are held
body.explanation: Adding any constraint can only shrink the set of portfolios the optimizer is allowed to choose from. The best a constrained solution can do is match the unconstrained optimum, when the constraint does not bind, and otherwise it must do strictly worse, exactly what this lesson's 17.5% and 18.0% examples showed.

A maximum allowed weight in one company or sector, such as SEBI's general 10% single-stock limit for most equity mutual fund schemes.

points: The no-short-selling constraint, w_i >= 0, is the realistic default for most Indian portfolios, given both cash-market structure and SEBI mutual fund rules.
Adding it back into the optimization can only match or worsen the unconstrained result. At an 18% target return, it cost this course's five-stock frontier 0.13 extra percentage points of risk.
As target return rises further, more assets hit their zero floor in sequence, which is why real tools solve constrained portfolios numerically rather than by hand-adjusting a closed-form formula.
SEBI's roughly 10% single-stock cap for most equity mutual fund schemes would have blocked every single holding in Chapter 4's five-stock tangency portfolio, a genuine, binding real-world limit.

Turnover has a real cost in India: brokerage, STT, and capital gains tax on every rebalancing trade, which is why most real portfolios trade some theoretical precision for a fixed schedule or a drift tolerance band instead of constant re-optimization.
None of these constraints mean the mean-variance framework from Chapters 3 and 4 was wrong. They mean the textbook solution is a starting point, not the final, tradeable answer.
